title: Word parts and breaking terms down
note: Most medical terms are built from a word root plus a prefix, a suffix, or both. A combining form is a root plus a linking vowel, usually o (gastr/o). To define a term, start with the suffix, then read the remaining parts from left to right.

read.title: Reading a term from the end
text: Medical words look long, but most are assembled from a small set of reusable parts. The word root carries the core meaning, often a body part: hepat means liver, nephr means kidney, oste means bone. A prefix can sit in front of the root to change its meaning, and a suffix sits at the end to say what is happening to it, such as inflammation, removal, or a recording.

Roots are usually learned as combining forms, which add a linking vowel, almost always o. The vowel is kept between two roots and before a suffix that starts with a consonant, so gastr/o plus -scope gives gastroscope. It is dropped before a suffix that starts with a vowel, so gastr/o plus -itis gives gastritis. Prefixes never need a linking vowel.

To define a term, read the suffix first, then go back to the beginning and read left to right. Osteoarthritis splits into oste/o, arthr/o and -itis: inflammation of bone and joint. Some terms, such as eponyms named for people and acronyms such as AIDS, cannot be decoded this way and simply have to be memorized.

q.q: In which order should you define the parts of a built term?
o: Prefix first, then the suffix, then the root
Suffix first, then the rest from left to right
Right to left through every part
